opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly one I think about a lot. The residual connection is a nice example because it looks almost trivially simple in hindsight: you add the input back to the output of a block. But its impact came from a whole chain of things around that simple idea.

First, I think current AI scientist systems are very good at local search. You give them a codebase and a metric, and they'll tweak hyperparameters, swap components, and write up the results. That's useful, but it's incremental. The residual connection wasn't really a hyperparameter tweak. It came from noticing a puzzling empirical phenomenon: deeper networks were doing *worse*, even on the training set. That's not overfitting, it's an optimization problem. Recognizing that something is surprising, that it contradicts what you'd expect, and then reframing the problem around it is the key step. Our systems still aren't great at noticing when something is genuinely weird versus just noise.

Second, there's the question of taste and problem selection. A lot of the value in research comes from picking the right question and knowing when to keep pushing on an idea that initially looks unpromising. Right now, most automated pipelines are fairly greedy. They optimize for a paper-sized result in a short horizon. To get something like residual connections, you need open-endedness: systems that maintain an archive of interesting stepping stones, explore ideas that don't immediately pay off, and come back to them later. That's very much the lesson from the open-endedness and quality-diversity literature.

Third, compute and scale of experimentation matter. The insight only became influential because it was validated at scale, across ImageNet and many architectures, and it then transferred to Transformers and basically everything else. An AI scientist needs to be able not just to propose an idea on a toy problem, but to test whether it generalizes and to understand *why* it works. That's where verification and good evaluation become critical, because otherwise you get a flood of papers that look plausible but don't hold up.

And finally, I think there's a social and communication side. A discovery becomes influential because the community adopts it. The ResNet paper had a clean story, a clear diagnosis, and a simple fix that anyone could implement. So AI scientists also need to get better at distilling: explaining the insight in a way that other researchers, human or machine, can build on.

So in short: better curiosity and anomaly detection, longer-horizon and more open-ended exploration, rigorous large-scale verification, and the ability to communicate a simple, general idea. We're seeing early pieces of all of these, but putting them together into a system that produces a residual-connection-level idea is still an open challenge, and a really exciting one.

r001.rationale: The response calls for rigorous large-scale testing and evaluation, but does not say that numerical experiment results guide what the system explores next.

r002.rationale: It mentions keeping an archive of stepping stones and validating ideas across architectures, but does not identify integrating knowledge across multiple experiments as a needed capability.

r003.rationale: It discusses noticing anomalies and reframing problems, but does not say the system should formulate new hypotheses from previous insights.

r004.rationale: The response mentions open-ended exploration and quality-diversity, but does not claim diversity and efficient scaling can suffice without post-training on experimental traces.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a really nice framing, because the residual connection is almost the perfect counterexample to how we usually think about discovery. It's not a big theoretical result. It's a few characters of code. You add the input back to the output of a block. And yet it's probably one of the two or three ideas that made deep learning scale at all, and it's in essentially every model we train today.

So the question is, what did it take for a human to find that, and what's missing from the systems we're building? And I think there are a few things.

The first is just the depth of the problem-finding. The people working on ResNets weren't trying to invent a new architecture component. They were trying to understand why deeper networks were getting worse, when in principle a deeper network should be able to represent anything a shallower one can. That's a very specific, almost paradoxical observation that bugs you. And a lot of current AI scientist systems, including the ones I've worked on, are quite good at the generate-and-test loop, but they're not yet good at sitting with a confusing observation and asking why it should be true. They tend to optimize a metric rather than chase an anomaly.

The second thing is the time horizon. The residual connection looks trivial in hindsight, but it came out of a long sequence of partial attempts, highway networks, initialization tricks, batch norm, and people iterating on the same frustration for years. Most of our systems right now operate on something like a one-shot or few-shot loop. You give it a research direction, it runs a bunch of experiments, it writes a paper. That's fine for incremental improvements, but influential discoveries usually come from sustained engagement with one problem, where you build up a lot of tacit knowledge about what fails and why. So I think we need systems with much longer-lived memory and the ability to maintain a research program over weeks or months, not hours.

The third point, and this is maybe the one I find most interesting, is taste for simplicity. One of the reasons the residual connection was so influential is that it was so simple that everyone could adopt it immediately. If you let an optimizer loose on architecture search, it will happily give you something complicated that gets you a half percent on a benchmark. That's not influence. Influence comes from finding the minimal intervention that explains a lot. And right now the reward signals we give these systems don't really reflect that. We reward benchmark numbers, we don't reward elegance or generality or how many other people would be able to use the idea.

And then there's the experimental infrastructure point, which is more mundane but I think underappreciated. The ResNet result needed a fairly expensive experiment to be convincing. You had to actually train a very deep network and show the trend reversing. An AI scientist that can only afford toy-scale experiments can discover things that are true at toy scale, and many of those don't transfer. So compute budget and the ability to design experiments that are cheap but predictive of large-scale behavior become a real scientific skill the system needs, not just an engineering detail.

So if I had to summarize, I'd say we need systems that can notice and hold onto a genuinely confusing observation, pursue it over a long horizon with accumulated knowledge, have a bias towards simple explanations rather than metric hacking, and have access to experiments that are actually informative about the regime we care about. I don't think any of those is impossible, and I'd argue we're making progress on each of them. But the current generation is still mostly a very fast, very tireless junior researcher. The residual connection needed something a bit more like stubbornness and taste.

r002.rationale: It says systems need long-lived memory and sustained work that builds accumulated, tacit knowledge about what fails and why across successive attempts.

astra-6.text:
I think they need the ability to question the setup, rather than just optimize within it. If you give an AI scientist a fixed benchmark and ask it to improve the score, it might become very good at searching architectures. But something like a residual connection involves finding a change in how you formulate the problem that makes a whole class of models easier to train.

So you want a system that can move between levels: look at an experiment, notice something unexpected, form a hypothesis about why it happened, and then design a small experiment that distinguishes that hypothesis from competing explanations. And it needs to be able to change its research agenda based on what it learns.

The difficult part is deciding what’s interesting. A failed experiment can contain a useful observation, but if your only feedback is the final benchmark score, you throw that away. I’d want these systems to build up an understanding across experiments, including the failures, and look for simple principles that transfer.

I don’t think we know yet whether that requires some fundamentally new ingredient or a much better integration of capabilities we already have. But generating more papers or running more experiments isn’t, by itself, the same thing as making a discovery.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they need a much better loop between generating an idea, running an experiment, and deciding what the result actually tells them. You can generate a lot of plausible architectural modifications, but that’s quite different from identifying a simple principle that works reliably and changes how people build models.

For something like a residual connection, the challenge is also knowing which problem to focus on. Where is the existing approach failing? What experiment would distinguish between competing explanations? And if an initial result is disappointing, is the idea wrong, or did you test it in the wrong setting? An AI scientist needs to make those judgments, rather than just execute a fixed research plan.

So I’d want systems with the ability to pursue a question over many experiments, revise their hypotheses, and build on what they’ve learned. More experiments help, but the important thing is whether those experiments make the system’s understanding better. That’s what could turn a large search over variations into a discovery.
